title: Cash Flow Statement
summary: A Cash Flow Statement, prepared as per AS-3 (Revised), shows the inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents during a period under operating, investing and financing activities. This chapter covers classification, the indirect method format and the usual adjustments.

notes.heading: Meaning, objectives and key terms
notes.html:
• Cash Flow Statement: a statement showing changes in cash and cash equivalents between two Balance Sheet dates, classified by activity.
  • Cash: cash in hand and demand deposits with banks.
  • Cash equivalents: short-term, highly liquid investments readily convertible into known amounts of cash with insignificant risk of change in value (maturity of 3 months or less from acquisition), e.g. treasury bills, commercial paper, short-term marketable securities.
  • Objectives: show sources and uses of cash, assess the ability to generate cash and pay dividends and debts, explain the gap between profit and cash, help in planning.
  • Limitations: ignores non-cash transactions and the accrual concept; not a substitute for the Statement of Profit and Loss; historical in nature.

notes.heading: Classification of activities
notes.html:
ActivityMeaningExamples
OperatingPrincipal revenue-producing activitiesCash sales, receipts from debtors, payments to suppliers and employees, income tax paid
InvestingPurchase and sale of long-term assets and investments not included in cash equivalentsPurchase/sale of machinery, land, non-current investments; interest and dividend received; loans given
FinancingChanges in the size and composition of owners' capital and borrowingsIssue of shares and debentures, redemption, loans raised/repaid, interest paid, dividend paid, bank overdraft and cash credit

Finance companies

For a financial enterprise (bank, NBFC), interest received and paid and dividend received are operating activities; dividend paid is still financing.

Non-cash transactions (not shown)

Issue of shares for machinery, conversion of debentures into shares, bonus shares, depreciation, cash deposited into bank (movement within cash and cash equivalents).

notes.heading: Format: indirect method
notes.html:
Particulars₹
A. Cash flows from operating activities
Net profit before tax and extraordinary items (see next section)
Add: non-cash and non-operating expenses (depreciation, goodwill written off, loss on sale of assets, interest on borrowings)
Less: non-operating incomes (interest and dividend received, profit on sale of assets)
Operating profit before working capital changes
Add: decrease in current assets, increase in current liabilities
Less: increase in current assets, decrease in current liabilities
Cash generated from operations
Less: income tax paid
Net cash from (used in) operating activities
B. Cash flows from investing activities
C. Cash flows from financing activities
Net increase/decrease in cash and cash equivalents (A + B + C)
Add: opening cash and cash equivalents
Closing cash and cash equivalents

Working capital changes exclude cash and cash equivalents, short-term borrowings (bank overdraft, cash credit: financing) and current investments treated as cash equivalents.

notes.heading: Net profit before tax and other key workings
notes.html:
Net profit before tax and extraordinary items = Closing balance of Surplus (Statement of P&L) − Opening balance + Transfer to reserves + Dividend paid/declared during the year (previous year's proposed dividend; interim dividend) + Provision for tax made during the year.

  • Provision for tax: if no other information is given, previous year's provision is the tax paid (outflow) and current year's provision is the amount provided (added back).
  • Proposed dividend: previous year's proposed dividend is paid in the current year (financing outflow, added back to profit). Current year's proposed dividend is only a note (contingent liability) and is ignored.
  • Fixed assets: prepare the asset account and accumulated depreciation account to find the missing purchase, sale proceeds or depreciation.
  • Interest on debentures/loans: add back in operating, show as outflow in financing.

notes.heading: Worked illustration
notes.html:
Information: Surplus rose from ₹1,00,000 to ₹1,80,000; transfer to General Reserve ₹20,000; provision for tax made ₹50,000; tax paid ₹45,000. Machinery (cost): opening ₹5,00,000, closing ₹6,40,000; accumulated depreciation: opening ₹1,00,000, closing ₹1,10,000. A machine costing ₹60,000 (accumulated depreciation ₹30,000) was sold for ₹25,000. Inventory increased by ₹30,000; trade receivables decreased by ₹10,000; trade payables increased by ₹15,000. Shares issued ₹1,00,000. Interest paid on debentures ₹10,000. Opening cash ₹30,000.

Workings: Loss on sale = (60,000 − 30,000) − 25,000 = 5,000. Depreciation charged = 1,10,000 + 30,000 − 1,00,000 = 40,000. Machinery purchased = 6,40,000 + 60,000 − 5,00,000 = 2,00,000.

Particulars₹
Net profit before tax (80,000 + 20,000 + 50,000)1,50,000
Add: Depreciation40,000
Add: Loss on sale of machinery5,000
Add: Interest on debentures10,000
Operating profit before working capital changes2,05,000
Less: Increase in inventory(30,000)
Add: Decrease in trade receivables10,000
Add: Increase in trade payables15,000
Cash generated from operations2,00,000
Less: Tax paid(45,000)
A. Net cash from operating activities1,55,000
Purchase of machinery(2,00,000)
Sale of machinery25,000
B. Net cash used in investing activities(1,75,000)
Issue of shares1,00,000
Interest paid(10,000)
C. Net cash from financing activities90,000
Net increase in cash (A + B + C)70,000
Add: Opening cash and cash equivalents30,000
Closing cash and cash equivalents1,00,000

notes.heading: Common mistakes
notes.html:
• Starting from profit after tax without adding back tax, dividend and transfers to reserves.
  • Treating bank overdraft as a working capital change; it is a financing activity.
  • Showing interest received under operating for a non-finance company (it is investing).
  • Showing the sale of a fixed asset at book value instead of the cash received.
  • Including non-cash transactions such as shares issued to vendors.
  • Treating depreciation as a source of cash: it is only added back because it was deducted without any cash outflow.

keyTerms.definition: Short-term, highly liquid investments with a maturity of three months or less, readily convertible into known amounts of cash.
The principal revenue-producing activities of the enterprise and other activities that are not investing or financing.
Acquisition and disposal of long-term assets and other investments not included in cash equivalents.
Activities that change the size and composition of owners' capital and borrowings.
Method that starts with net profit before tax and adjusts it for non-cash, non-operating items and working capital changes.
A transaction with no inflow or outflow of cash, such as issue of shares for assets; excluded from the statement.
Non-recurring events not from ordinary activities, such as loss by earthquake or an insurance claim received; disclosed separately.
The accounting standard that governs the preparation of the Cash Flow Statement.

formulas.name: Net profit before tax
formulas.html: Increase in Surplus + Transfer to reserves + Dividend paid + Provision for tax made

formulas.name: Cash generated from operations
formulas.html: Operating profit before working capital changes ± Changes in current assets and current liabilities

formulas.name: Net cash from operating activities
formulas.html: Cash generated from operations − Income tax paid

formulas.name: Asset purchased (cost basis)
formulas.html: Closing balance + Cost of asset sold − Opening balance

formulas.name: Depreciation charged
formulas.html: Closing accumulated depreciation + Accumulated depreciation on asset sold − Opening accumulated depreciation

formulas.name: Closing cash
formulas.html: Opening cash and cash equivalents + Net cash from operating, investing and financing activities

mcqs.explanation: AS-3 (Revised) deals with cash flow statements.

mcqs.q: Dividend received by a manufacturing company is a cash flow from
mcqs.explanation: It is a return on investment, so it is an investing inflow for a non-finance company.

mcqs.q: Interest paid on debentures by a trading company is shown under
mcqs.explanation: It is the cost of raising finance.

mcqs.q: Which of the following will not result in a flow of cash?
options: Issue of shares to the vendor of a building
mcqs.explanation: It is a non-cash transaction: no cash moves.

mcqs.q: Machinery with a book value of ₹80,000 was sold at a loss of ₹15,000. The inflow under investing activities is
While computing cash from operating activities, an increase in trade receivables is
mcqs.explanation: More money is tied up in debtors, so cash is lower than profit.

mcqs.q: Opening provision for tax ₹40,000; closing provision ₹55,000; tax paid ₹35,000. Provision made during the year is

Assertion (A): Depreciation is added back to net profit while calculating cash from operating activities.
Reason (R): Depreciation is a non-cash expense.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: It reduced profit without any cash outflow, so it is added back.

questions.q: State whether 'cash deposited into bank' results in an inflow, outflow or no flow of cash, with reason.
questions.answerHtml: No flow. It is only a movement between two components of cash and cash equivalents.

questions.q: Classify into operating, investing and financing activities for a manufacturing company: (i) purchase of patents; (ii) payment of wages; (iii) repayment of long-term loan.
questions.answerHtml:
• (i) Purchase of patents: investing (acquisition of a long-term asset).
  • (ii) Payment of wages: operating (principal revenue-producing activity).
  • (iii) Repayment of long-term loan: financing (change in borrowings).

questions.q: Calculate net profit before tax: Surplus (opening) ₹2,00,000; Surplus (closing) ₹3,10,000; Transfer to General Reserve ₹40,000; Previous year's proposed dividend paid ₹60,000; Provision for tax made during the year ₹90,000.
questions.answerHtml:
Particulars₹
Increase in Surplus (3,10,000 − 2,00,000)1,10,000
Add: Transfer to General Reserve40,000
Add: Dividend paid60,000
Add: Provision for tax90,000
Net profit before tax3,00,000

questions.q: From the following, calculate cash flows from investing activities: Machinery (at cost) opening ₹8,00,000, closing ₹10,00,000; Accumulated depreciation opening ₹2,00,000, closing ₹2,60,000. During the year a machine costing ₹1,00,000, on which accumulated depreciation was ₹40,000, was sold at a profit of ₹10,000. Non-current investments were purchased for ₹50,000 and interest of ₹6,000 was received on them.
questions.answerHtml:
Workings: Book value of machine sold = 1,00,000 − 40,000 = 60,000; sale proceeds = 60,000 + 10,000 = ₹70,000.

Machinery purchased = 10,00,000 + 1,00,000 − 8,00,000 = ₹3,00,000.

Particulars₹
Purchase of machinery(3,00,000)
Sale of machinery70,000
Purchase of non-current investments(50,000)
Interest received6,000
Net cash used in investing activities(2,74,000)

questions.q: Calculate cash flows from operating activities: Net profit before tax ₹4,00,000; Depreciation ₹60,000; Goodwill written off ₹20,000; Profit on sale of land ₹30,000; Interest on debentures ₹24,000; Dividend received ₹14,000. Changes: Inventories increased by ₹40,000; Trade receivables increased by ₹25,000; Trade payables increased by ₹35,000; Outstanding expenses decreased by ₹5,000; Bank overdraft increased by ₹50,000. Income tax paid ₹80,000.
questions.answerHtml:
Particulars₹
Net profit before tax4,00,000
Add: Depreciation60,000
Add: Goodwill written off20,000
Add: Interest on debentures24,000
Less: Profit on sale of land(30,000)
Less: Dividend received(14,000)
Operating profit before working capital changes4,60,000
Less: Increase in inventories(40,000)
Less: Increase in trade receivables(25,000)
Add: Increase in trade payables35,000
Less: Decrease in outstanding expenses(5,000)
Cash generated from operations4,25,000
Less: Income tax paid(80,000)
Net cash from operating activities3,45,000

Note: the increase in bank overdraft is a financing activity and is not adjusted here.
